text: So what does it take to build and deploy an AI agent in the physical world at scale?
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Now in Silicon Valley, there's a common mantra to move fast and break things.

text: However, when you're dealing with atoms instead of bits, breaking things is not really okay.

text: So the thing you have to do is to move fast and ship safely.

text: And that's a much more difficult thing to do.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: You have to build systems that are robust from day one.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: You have to build AI models and you have to build training recipes where safety is the foundation and not an afterthought, not an add-on.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And by the way, the problem itself of physical AI is different from digital AI.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There are four main gaps that you have to contend with if you're building AI for the physical world versus the digital world.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: First, there is the cost of error gaps.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: If you have a language model or a chatbot or a copilot and it makes a mistake, usually it costs you a retry.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In the physical world, the cost of a mistake can be measured in human lives, not tokens.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There's simply not an undo and a retry button.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Secondly, you have the latency gap.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And typically, when you're running a vLM or a digital assistant, it can take many seconds, sometimes minutes, to come back with an answer to you.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: A car traveling at freeway speeds moves about 100 feet in one second.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: So their milliseconds really matter.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And you have to run all of your inference, make all of your decisions on board a compute that fits in the trunk of your car.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Next, there's the data gap.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Digital AI had the internet of this wonderful, immense cache of pre-labeled human knowledge and human thought that we've ever assembled.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: There's no digitized version of the internet for the physical world.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And lastly, there's the validation gap.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In digital AI, often you can ship something that's good enough.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And then you let your users use your product, they find the edge cases, and that allows you to deploy on day one practically at unlimited scale.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And then you can just iterate and hill climb on quality from there.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: In physical AI, the situation is different.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: Given the high cost of errors,
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: You need to have a very high level of safety and a very high level of confidence on day one before you deploy your first robot, before you drive your first autonomous mile.

text: Now, at the same time, when you're dealing with physical AI,

text: The first lesson has to do with this massive, frustrating, sometimes soul-crushing difference between a demo and a real product.

text: And at scale,
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: The long tail is the problem space.

text: It's your entire problem statement.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: When you drive millions of miles per week, a rare event that might happen once in a million miles, that just becomes your daily reality.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And getting those next nines
speaker: SPEAKER_02

speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: So you don't get to say six nines of performance or reliability by doing the same thing that you did to achieve the first two, but longer.

text: You can get to the first couple of nines by just doing proper engineering and doing some bug fixes.

text: And the same thing holds for the performance of AI models.

text: So what that actually means is that in this space, it's incredibly easy to get started, but it can be excruciatingly difficult to get to the real product.
speaker: SPEAKER_02

text: And that effect is only amplified with every wave of technological breakthroughs.

text: Now, this being a startup school, the last thing I want to do is throw too much cold water on the magic and the excitement of those early days.

text: Otherwise, you might be in for a pretty rude awakening later.
